tier_reason: The README gives first-party speed claims with no published results table, hardware, runtime version or methodology. A harness exists (test-base64.js, run with `npx chrodemon`) but its output is never published.

corrections.baseline: The package's own pure-JS port (fast-base64/js), which the README says is 'the fastest existing JS implementation', plus native atob()/btoa() through its own fast-base64/nano wrapper
corrections.claimed_speedup: "~20x faster than the fastest JS implementation on the first 100kB of input" and "~2-3x faster than the fastest JS on the first 100MB" (the 'fastest JS' being the package's own fast-base64/js). The README also lists relative slowdowns against the default Wasm+SIMD build: fast-base64/js is '2-30x slower' and the atob/btoa-based fast-base64/nano is '3-100x slower'. Its one absolute example is 10kB of base64 decoding in 0.06ms with fast-base64 vs 5ms with nano on the author's laptop.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 58 stars; npm fast-base64 had 6,003 downloads in the week of 2026-09-19 to 2026-09-25 (latest version 0.1.8)
corrections.caveats: The 'fastest JS implementation' baseline is the author's own pure-JS port shipped in the same package. The README says so, but it is not an independent library. Native atob()/btoa() only appears through the nano wrapper, which adds array/string conversion overhead. No hardware, browser/Node version or results table is given, and the harness (test-base64.js) prints timings without publishing them. It cannot be used directly from C++ (JS/Wasm only) and is included under the any-language allowance.

notes: The README numbers match the record word for word. The README also clarifies that the 'fastest JS implementation' is the package's own fast-base64/js, so I corrected the baseline and caveats. Metadata checks out: MIT, 58 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2022-01-04 (abandoned).

tier_reason: These are the author's own blog numbers on a named CPU (M1 at 3.2GHz). The companion test gist (a15a0fe, main.cpp) has a timing harness and a clang++ -O3 build line, but the harness does not run zlib: zlib's ~30GB/s was measured separately and its code is not published. The clang version is not stated either.

corrections.claimed_speedup: The original 12-chain test code runs at 'about 70GB/s on the M1, reaching up to 75GB/s if the assembly is adjusted to always have valid fusion pairs', vs the zlib crc32 function at 'around 30GB/s' on the same M1 (~2.3x, derived from page data). This gist is the 'slightly cleaner/faster version using inline assembly and C++ templates' and 'reaches ~76GB/s'. The CRC32X instruction's theoretical best case is 25.6GB/s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang++ -std=c++17 -O3 (build comment in the companion test-code gist a15a0feac92e2126932b0fbe1de7863d/main.cpp; clang version not stated; this gist has no build line)
corrections.workload: CRC32/CRC32C throughput on large buffers (author profiled 128KB and up; the test harness uses 2 MiB) on the Apple M1. It uses PMULL/PMULL2+EOR folding with 12 independent latency chains, building on Intel's 2009 PCLMULQDQ folding technique.
corrections.caveats: Distributed only as GitHub gists with an 'AS IS' warranty disclaimer and no license grant. The zlib comparison was measured separately and is not in the published harness, which checks correctness against a slice-by-4 table CRC. The speed depends on PMULL+EOR fusion, which the author says is likely unique to Apple-designed CPUs. The author also says it may hurt performance on small buffers and that the test code is 'not suitable for real-world use as-is'. By the author's 2024 update it is superseded by corsix/fast-crc32 (85GB/s on M1, ~10% faster, already catalogued).

notes: The blog numbers match the record. 70/75GB/s belong to the original test gist (a15a0fe), and the cleaner version under this record's URL reaches ~76GB/s. The gist file is crc32.cpp (C++ templates plus inline asm), so the record's language 'C' should be C++; that field is not correctable here. I changed maintenance to abandoned because the code was last touched 2022-06-06 and the author never calls it complete. HN story 31469295 has 343 points, as the record says.

tier_reason: The README table gives first-party cargo-bench results on an M1 MacBook, and the bench code is public (src/lib.rs, tests::benchmark, 12 MiB of random data). The rustc version and flags are not stated, and the author calls the machine noisy.

corrections.claimed_speedup: neon_tbl 6.24 GiB/s vs byte_by_byte 0.79 GiB/s (~7.9x, derived from page data); portable_simd 3.46 GiB/s (~4.4x, derived from page data). The best single run was 1,794,971 ns for 12 MiB, i.e. 6.53 GiB/s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust nightly required (#![feature(portable_simd)] and #![feature(test)] in src/lib.rs); rustc version and flags not stated
corrections.caveats: The author says the benchmark machine was noisy ('on battery power, so take these results with a grain of salt'). The baseline is the repo's own naive scalar loop (branchy per-nibble, uppercase output), not a named hex library such as the hex crate. It needs nightly Rust. The author calls it a coding exercise to learn cargo bench and inline assembly.

notes: The README numbers match the record, and I marked the ratio as derived. Metadata checks out: GPL-3.0, 0 stars, not a fork, last commit 2023-01-25 (abandoned). The in-repo scalar baseline is kept, following the precedent of other own-scalar-baseline encoding entries.
